snp3.6:6.3: Reading daharo’pi c’esa samaṇo Gotamo mahiddhiko hoti mahānubhāvo, following the Burmese edition.
snp3.6:13.5: Many of the Buddha’s answers to Sabhiya play on sound as well as sense; this verse plays on bhikkhu (monk), bhavaṁ (becoming), and khīṇa- (ended).
snp3.6:14.4: Ussada: according to SnA, this covers such defilements as passion, aversion, delusion, pride, and conceit. See Sn 4:14.
snp3.6:15.2: I.e., dispassionate toward the sense faculties and their objects. See SN 35:153.
snp3.6:15.4: An image drawn out more fully at Thag 11 and Thag 14:1, comparing one who awaits death without delighting either in death or in living to a worker mindfully awaiting his wage.
snp3.6:16.4: This verse contains an end-rhyme, visuddhaṁ/Buddhaṁ, which is rare in Pali poetry.
snp3.6:19.1: Alliteration between bāhetvā (banished) and brahmā (brahman, shortened to fit the meter); a similar alliteration is found at Dhp 388 and Ud 1:4–5.
snp3.6:21.4: Alliteration between n’eti (doesn’t come/go) and nhātako (washed). Also a play on words—normally a person is washed of dirt, but here the arahant is washed of theory.
snp3.6:22.1: The Pali āguṁ na karoti could be rephrased na āguṁ karoti, yielding a play on the word nāga, as at AN 6:43. Since nāga can also mean “large elephant,” the verse further plays on the image of one freed from all fetters and bonds.
snp3.6:25.1: SnA cites AN 3:77 to identify “field” with kamma: kamma is the field, consciousness the seed, and craving the moisture.
snp3.6:26.1: As with “field,” SnA identifies “storehouses” as storehouses of kamma; alliteration between kosāni (storehouses) and kusalo (skillful).
snp3.6:27.1: SnA glosses “white flowers” as the six sense media, normally pure yet capable of growth (see SN 22:54); it may also refer to states of mind marked by a perception of whiteness, such as the white-totality and the mastery described at AN 10:29—though even that mastery is said to still involve aberration and change, so the verse here points beyond all states of darkness and brightness. The line also carries an alliteration—white flowers (paṇḍarāni) and wise (paṇḍito)—that survives into English.
snp3.6:31.4: A play on words between vedāni (knowledges) and vedanā (feelings).
snp3.6:33.4: Reading vīro with GD rather than dhīro, found in the printed editions but a poor fit here. This gives the verse three alliterated words: virato (abstaining), viriyavā (one with persistence), and vīro (hero).
snp3.6:37.1: Two senses of the single word abhiññāya: “having directly known” and “for the sake of direct knowing.”
snp3.6:37.5: Alliteration between sutavā (having heard) and sottiyo (learned).
snp3.6:38.3: SnA identifies “mud” as the strings of sensuality, and the three types of perception as beginning with the perception of sensuality—either sensuality, ill-will, & harmfulness, or sensuality, form, & formlessness. This verse also alliterates ālayāni (attachments) and ariyo (noble).
snp3.6:42.1: According to SnA, the 63 wrong views comprise the 62 listed at DN 1 together with the wrong view of self-identity (sakkāya-diṭṭhi).
snp3.6:47.3: According to SnA, these are classes of devas noted for their discernment.
snp3.6:51.6: The word “feet”—pāde—functions as a lamp-word here.
snp3.6:54.4: vv. 510–547. See also: DN 2; Ud 1:9; Thag 6:9.
